title: Daytime Darkness! A Total Solar Eclipse Is Coming to Spain and Iceland
summary: Imagine the sun vanishing in the middle of the day! On August 12, a total solar eclipse will turn daytime into darkness for people in Spain, Iceland, and Greenland. For up to 2 minutes and 18 seconds, the moon will perfectly cover the sun. This is the first time in more than 100 years that mainland Spain will see a total eclipse. The moon's shadow will race across 5,130 miles (8,260 kilometers) — that's like crossing the United States almost twice! Most of this path is over the Atlantic Ocean. The best view will be off Iceland's west coast. In Spain, crowds will see about one minute of darkness. Even if you're not in the path, you might see a partial eclipse. In Dublin, 94% of the sun will be covered. In New York, it's just a 9% bite. Remember: never look at the sun without special eclipse glasses! But wait, there's more! That same morning, six planets — including Jupiter and Mars — will line up in the sky before dawn. Then, after sunset, the Perseid meteor shower will peak under a dark, moonless sky. You might even spot a shooting star during the eclipse! Scientists are super excited. They'll launch over 60 high-altitude balloons from Spain and Iceland to study how the eclipse cools the air. A NASA plane will chase the eclipse at 460 mph (740 kph) to take thousands of pictures of the sun's outer atmosphere, called the corona. Michael Zeiler, an eclipse expert, will watch from a cruise ship in a Greenland fjord. He's hoping to see the northern lights during totality — that would be a rare double show!
why_it_matters: Seeing a total solar eclipse is a once-in-a-lifetime experience that can spark a lifelong interest in science and space exploration.

background_read: A total solar eclipse happens when the moon moves directly between Earth and the sun, casting a dark shadow on the ground.
The last time mainland Spain experienced a total eclipse was in 1905, so this is a rare event for people there.
NASA (the American space agency) is sending a special plane to fly along the eclipse path and take thousands of pictures of the sun's corona.
Article_Structure: WHO: People in Spain, Iceland, and Greenland, plus scientists like Michael Zeiler.
WHAT: A total solar eclipse will turn day to night for up to 2 minutes 18 seconds on August 12.
WHERE: Along a path from Spain to Iceland and Greenland, mostly over the Atlantic Ocean.
WHY: Because total eclipses are rare in these areas; scientists want to study the sun's corona and how the eclipse cools the air.

perspectives.description: Sky-watchers and scientists are thrilled by the rare chance to see the eclipse and other events like the Perseid meteor shower.
Looking directly at the sun can hurt your eyes, so everyone must use special eclipse glasses.
For researchers, the eclipse is a natural experiment to learn more about the sun's atmosphere and Earth's weather.
